not.text: The board doesn't regularly discuss, or get reports on, the security of the systems behind your essential functions.
When the board discusses security, it works from incomplete or outdated information, with no expert advice.
The board's direction doesn't effectively drive how those systems are secured in practice.
Senior managers or some teams think certain security policies don't apply to them, or expect exceptions.

achieved.text: The board owns your security approach and policy, and explains it meaningfully to risk decision-makers across the organisation.
The board regularly discusses security using timely, accurate information and expert advice.
One board member is accountable overall for security and keeps it regularly on the board's agenda.
The board's direction is turned into real working practices that control how systems are secured.
The board understands how system security supports your essential functions, and what a compromise would mean.
Security is seen as key to keeping essential functions running, and is part of every relevant discussion.

not.text: Key security roles are missing, vacant, or covered informally or only as and when needed.
People are given security duties without the authority or resources to carry them out.
Staff don't know what they are responsible for in keeping essential functions secure.

achieved.text: You have identified key security roles and responsibilities, and regularly review that they're still right.
Those roles are filled by capable, knowledgeable people with the time, authority and resources to do them.
It is clear who is accountable overall for the security of these systems.

not.text: Simple risk decisions keep getting passed up the chain, or never get made.
Local teams handle risks informally, or ignore them, when they should be reported through the formal risk process.
Decision-makers don't clearly know how much risk senior management will accept, beyond vague words like "cautious".
Decision-makers can't explain why they made their risk decisions.
Teams make risk decisions in silos, e.g. engineering and IT don't talk to each other about risk.
Risk ratings are too vague to prioritise, e.g. nearly everything is "medium" or "amber".

achieved.text: Senior management can see the key risk decisions being made across the organisation.
Decision-makers know they must make timely, effective risk decisions that stay within the level of risk senior management has said it will accept.
Risk decisions are handed down, or passed up, to whoever has the skills, knowledge, tools and authority to make them.
Past risk decisions are regularly reviewed to check they're still relevant and valid.

not.text: Risk assessments don't start from a clear, agreed view of who might attack you and what they could do.
Risk assessment results are too complex for decision-makers, and aren't communicated clearly or promptly.
Risk assessments are done once and never revisited, or not done at all.
Projects treat finishing a risk assessment as a box to tick, ignoring what it actually found.
There's no systematic process to make sure identified security risks are actually dealt with.
Systems are assessed on their own, ignoring how they rely on or connect to others, e.g. office IT and the operational technology (OT) that runs physical equipment.
Security controls are chosen at random or copied from a standard list, without asking how each one actually helps protect your essential functions.
Risks sit unresolved on the register for long periods, waiting for senior decisions or resources.

partial.text: You have a process that identifies, analyses, prioritises and manages security risks to essential functions.
Your risk assessments draw on an understanding of well-known threats and vulnerabilities in your systems.
Your risk process produces a clear set of security requirements that address the risks found.
Important findings from your risk process are shared with key security decision-makers and accountable people.
You reassess risk after significant changes, e.g. a system replacement, new technology or a change in threat.

achieved.text: You have a process that identifies, analyses, prioritises and manages security risks to essential functions.
Your risk thinking centres on how attackers could disrupt your essential functions, and how the way your systems are secured would help or hinder them.
Your risk assessments start from a clear view of who might attack you and how, kept up to date for your systems, your sector and national infrastructure more widely.
Your risk assessments draw on an understanding of the vulnerabilities in your systems.
Your risk process produces prioritised security requirements, each of which can be traced back to the risk it addresses.
Important findings from your risk process are shared with key security decision-makers and accountable people.
Your risk assessments are living documents, updated promptly when systems, their use, technology or threats change.
You regularly review how well your risk process works, and improve it as needed.
You look ahead to new technologies that attackers could use against your systems.

not.text: You're unable to work out who might attack your systems, how, and why.
You don't understand the threats to the systems behind your essential functions.
You don't have a clear, agreed view of who might attack you and what they could do.
You don't use what you know about threats when making risk decisions.

partial.text: You work out who might attack your systems and understand how common, everyday attacks would affect them.
You understand common types of cyber attack and how they might affect your systems, and keep this up to date.
You can predict what attackers might target in your systems to harm your essential functions.
Your understanding of threats is shaped by the kinds of incidents that commonly happen.
You use what you know about threats when making risk decisions.

achieved.text: You analyse in detail who might attack your systems and how, taking into account your sector and national infrastructure more widely.
You understand how capable, well-resourced attackers could systematically use their methods against your systems.
You look at your systems from an attacker's point of view and build realistic attack scenarios.
You understand the steps a capable, well-resourced attacker would need to take to reach their likely targets.
You identify, and can justify, measures that make it harder for an attacker to succeed at each step.
You keep a detailed, current understanding of threats, e.g. through threat intelligence and research.
You use your detailed understanding of threats when making risk decisions.
You have written down the steps for carrying out a detailed analysis of who might attack you and how.

not.text: A product or service is treated as a cure-all, and vendor claims are accepted without checking.
Security checks such as audits, tests or certifications are relied on without understanding what each one can and can't prove.
You assume security is fine because nothing has gone wrong yet.

achieved.text: You check that your security measures work, and keep working for as long as they're needed.
You know the different ways of gaining confidence in your security, such as testing, audits and certification, and pick the ones that suit your systems.
You can justify your confidence in security across technology, people and processes, and a third party could verify it.
Weaknesses found by these checks are assessed, prioritised and fixed promptly and effectively where needed.
You review how you check your security, to make sure those checks work and are still the best choice.

not.text: Your lists of relevant assets are incomplete, missing or lack detail.
Only some areas or types of asset are recorded and understood.
You don't understand how assets rely on each other, e.g. between office IT and the operational technology (OT) that runs physical equipment.
Information, including personal or critical data, is kept for long periods without a business need or retention policy.
Only one or two people hold knowledge critical to running or recovering your systems, with no succession plan.
Asset lists are neglected and out of date.

achieved.text: All relevant assets are identified and listed in suitable detail, and the list is kept up to date.
You recognise and record dependencies on supporting infrastructure, such as power and cooling.
You have ranked your assets by how important they are to running the systems behind your essential functions.
Every relevant asset, including physical ones, has someone responsible for managing it.
Assets are managed with security in mind throughout their life, from when they're created or bought to when they're retired or disposed of.

not.text: You don't know which of your data suppliers hold, or how they manage it.
Parts of your supply chain are subcontracted and you have little or no visibility of those subcontractors.
You don't know which contracts matter for security, or they lack proper security obligations.
Suppliers' access to your systems is unrestricted, unmonitored or bypasses your security controls.

partial.text: You understand the general risks suppliers may pose to your systems.
You know how far your supply chain extends, including subcontractors.
Suppliers can show their cyber security is at the right level to cope with common threats.
You know which contracts matter for security and include appropriate security obligations in them.
You know about every connection third parties have into your systems, and have evidence that each one meets your security requirements.
Your incident management plans cover incidents that might start in your supply chain.
You're confident suppliers protect information they hold that your systems need from common threats.

achieved.text: You deeply understand your supply chain, including subcontractors, and the wider risks it faces.
Your risk assessments and buying decisions weigh suppliers' ownership, nationality, partners, subcontractors and security approach.
Your supply chain risk planning considers capable, well-resourced attackers deliberately compromising your suppliers to get at you.
Your most important suppliers can show their cyber security is at the right level to withstand capable, well-resourced attackers.
You're confident suppliers protect information essential to your systems from capable, well-resourced attackers.
You know which contracts matter for security and include appropriate security obligations in them.
You actively manage relevant contracts, which may include a contract management plan.
Contracts set out which responsibilities belong to you and which to the supplier.
All network connections and data sharing with third parties are well managed, with controls that match the level of risk.
Where appropriate, you and your suppliers support each other in resolving incidents.

not.text: Your software suppliers don't know what their software contains or where its components came from.
Software, including updates and patches, gets little or no testing.
Updates and patches often cause new problems or don't fix existing ones.
Vulnerabilities are found in software that could easily have been prevented.

partial.text: Your software supplier follows secure development principles and practices.
Your software suppliers can show at least a basic understanding of what their software contains and where it came from.
Development, test and production environments, code and repositories are protected well enough to withstand common threats.
Testing uses a range of methods across the whole development process, checking both what the software does and qualities such as performance and security.
You've arranged to get timely security updates, patches and notifications from your software supplier.
You get software, updates and patches from suppliers in a way that stops them being intercepted or tampered with.
Your software suppliers have processes to find, report and fix security vulnerabilities.
Your software supplier will tell you about significant events that could harm your systems.
If you use open-source software, you've taken sensible steps, scaled to the risk, to become confident in its security and stay that way.
You have appropriate support and maintenance arrangements in place.

achieved.text: Your software suppliers follow a recognised secure development framework, such as NIST SSDF or Microsoft SDL.
Your supplier knows exactly what goes into its software, including third-party components, and watches those components for new vulnerabilities for the product's whole life.
Development, test and production environments, code and repositories are protected well enough to withstand capable, well-resourced attackers.
Software development is shaped by a current understanding of threats, using techniques like threat modelling (mapping out how someone might attack it) to find weaknesses.
You can confirm software, updates and patches are genuine and haven't been tampered with.
